title: Procurement auctions: New bidders discipline incumbent prices
desc: Finds entrant participation can lower prices without winning work, distinguishing competitive pressure from demonstrated gains in overall value.

kps.k: Legal procurement can benefit from new bidders without shifting work to them: competitive pressure on incumbents is the central mechanism.
kps.d: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions argues that open-ended auctions let buyers retain award discretion rather than commit to a disclosed quality–price scoring rule. In the model, uncertainty about selection prompts incumbents to cut prices to avoid losing to cheaper, lower-quality entrants. Higher-quality incumbents retain winning positions, improving the quality of incumbent winners through selection. These are conditional theoretical results, not claims that every entrant improves procurement outcomes; the quality result requires sufficiently small cost-efficiency differences among incumbents. Bidding alone need not change equilibrium outcomes.

qs.q: However, the uncertainty in the buyer’s ﬁnal award decision in an open-ended format makes it suboptimal for the incumbents to keep their prices high: they bid more aggressively than they would in a closed-ended auction to minimize the risk of losing to low-price nonincumbents.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

qs.q: The highest quality incumbents hold on to winning spots, and lower-quality incumbents lose out.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

kps.k: The empirical evidence shows lower prices, but entrant awards do not necessarily improve overall value.
kps.d: The study examines GECF’s first online legal-services auctions following its 2003 switch from negotiated incumbent awards. Separate service categories and quantitative buyer quality assessments support a before-and-after comparison, rather than a randomized test. The authors report price savings for both incumbent and nonincumbent winners. In auctions with a nonincumbent winner, average pre-auction hourly rates were $320.73 versus $286.06 for the present value of nonincumbent winners’ rates. Yet entrants’ quality losses offset their savings in the Composite Score, yielding no significant direct overall benefit. The authors locate the main gains in lower bids and better quality-adjusted scores among incumbent winners.

qs.q: Our data come from the ﬁrst online auctions after this switch.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

qs.q: For the auctions where there was at least one nonincumbent supplier winner, the average before-auction hourly rate was $320.73; the average present value of the nonincumbent winner’s hourly rates in contrast was $286.06.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Apparent incumbency advantages may reflect buyer preferences for quality rather than favoritism.
kps.d: The authors contrast their results with earlier manufacturing-procurement research reporting an incumbent winning advantage. Their logit regressions account for buyer quality assessments, final bids and bidding-room competition. They find that the apparent incumbency advantage can disappear after quality controls and report no discretionary favoritism toward incumbents in this setting. This challenges an interpretation of repeat awards as incumbency bias, but does not establish that incumbency never matters across legal procurement or other markets.

qs.q: Incumbency and Winner Selection To test Hypothesis 3, we conduct a series of logit regressions, controlling for the relevant factors including the buyer’s assessment of supplier service quality.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

qs.q: We show that when one takes quality into account, what may look like incumbency advantage may disappear.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

kps.k: Nonbinding scoring weights may misrepresent how buyers actually trade quality against price.
kps.d: The study reports a significant difference between announced scoring preferences and preferences inferred from final supplier selection. This matters when assessing procurement success: advertised weights do not necessarily capture the buyer’s actual valuation of outcomes. The authors separately hypothesize improved utility measured using revealed preferences; that hypothesis should not be treated as an empirical finding merely because the stated-versus-revealed difference was supported.

qs.q: We ﬁnd that the buyer’s revealed preferences signiﬁcantly differ from her stated preferences.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

qs.q: Further, again based on Proposition 3, the buyer’s average utility based on her revealed preferences should also be improved compared to her utility before.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

kps.k: The practical recommendation is conditional auction design with continued supplier diversification.
kps.d: The authors favor open-ended auctions mixing incumbents and entrants when buyers place strong weight on quality and supplier cost differences remain relatively small. They favor simpler, binding scoring rules for generic, less critical purchases with similar suppliers. Repeated awards to high-quality firms could concentrate supply and worsen future prices, so buyers should maintain supplier diversity. Proposed applications to consulting, IT outsourcing and manufacturing extend the argument beyond the observed legal-services setting; they do not constitute evidence from those markets.

qs.q: In particular, in service or product markets where the buyer’s preference for quality is strong (even at its lowest possible value on its support) and the cost differences among suppliers are relatively low, open-ended auctions should be successful for the buyers, and with the mix of new suppliers and incumbent suppliers, open-ended auctions could reduce prices while maintaining quality.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

qs.q: Simpler closed-ended auctions would more likely be desirable for more generic and less critical parts of a product for which quality may carry a relatively lower weight than cost savings and where the suppliers are relatively similar and none of them exhibits strong quality-based advantages over others.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Its theoretical mechanism is that entrant participation disciplines incumbent pricing: in an open-ended auction, uncertainty over the buyer’s final selection gives incumbents an incentive to bid more aggressively to avoid losing to lower-priced entrants. Its empirical analysis also supports the proposition’s distinction between competitive pressure and demonstrated overall value. Although entrant winners offered lower prices, their quality losses offset those savings in the study’s Composite Score; the principal benefit instead arose indirectly through lower incumbent bids and improved selection among incumbent suppliers. This is qualified rather than mixed support: the source does not claim that auctions or entrants invariably improve procurement. Results depend on award discretion, quality sensitivity, supplier cost differences and continued supplier diversification, and switching to bidding alone need not change outcomes. Because the curated evidence contains one academic source, it does not establish the prevalence of this view within academia or permit assessment of variation between academic sources; the material variation is within the study’s own conditional findings.

qs.q: However, the uncertainty in the buyer’s ﬁnal award decision in an open-ended format makes it suboptimal for the incumbents to keep their prices high: they bid more aggressively than they would in a closed-ended auction to minimize the risk of losing to low-price nonincumbents.

qs.q: That is, there is no signiﬁcant direct overall beneﬁt for the buyer from the nonincumbent suppliers, as the price beneﬁt they bring is negated overall (as measured by the Composite Score) by the loss in quality of service when they win the contracts.
qs.a: An Empirical Analysis of Price, Quality, and Incumbency in Procurement Auctions · Academia · 2014

elens.an: The pre-2015 source directly supports the proposition that new bidders can benefit legal procurement chiefly by disciplining incumbent prices, even when entrants do not win the work. Its theoretical model attributes this effect specifically to open-ended auctions: uncertainty about the buyer’s final quality–price trade-off induces incumbents to bid more aggressively against lower-priced entrants. Its empirical analysis is consistent with lower prices, while distinguishing that competitive-pressure benefit from the value of awarding work to entrants. Material internal variation qualifies rather than reverses the support: entrant winners’ price savings were offset by lower service quality in the Composite Score, so direct overall benefit was not significant; the mechanism depends on auction design, strong buyer quality preferences, and relatively limited cost differences; and repeated incumbent success may create supplier concentration. Because this curated period contains only this study, the finding should be treated as evidence from its particular legal-services procurement setting, not as a measure of how broadly the view was held or as proof that all procurement auctions have the same effects.
